Gordon Setter.summary: The heaviest of the setters, a black-and-tan Scottish bird dog made famous by the 4th Duke of Gordon.
funFacts: The breed was developed at Gordon Castle in the 1820s.
It's the only black-and-tan setter breed.

Great Dane.summary: A giant German breed once used to hunt wild boar, now known as the "Apollo of dogs" for its gentle, patient nature.
funFacts: A Great Dane named Zeus was the tallest dog on record, 44 inches at the shoulder.
Scooby-Doo and Marmaduke are both Great Danes.

Great Pyrenees.summary: A large, white livestock guardian from the Pyrenees mountains, bred to protect sheep from wolves and bears.
funFacts: King Louis XIV reportedly named it the Royal Dog of France in 1675.
Like the Beauceron and Briard, it has double dewclaws on its hind legs.

Greater Swiss Mountain Dog.summary: The largest and oldest of the Swiss mountain dogs, a strong tricolor drafter once called "the poor man's horse."
funFacts: It pulled heavy carts of meat and dairy for farmers and butchers.
It's the largest of the four Swiss Sennenhund breeds.

Greyhound.summary: The fastest dog breed, a sleek sighthound with ancient roots, often adopted today as a gentle retired racer.
funFacts: Greyhounds can reach about 45 mph.
Despite their speed, they're famous for lounging indoors — fans call them "45-mph couch potatoes."

Havanese.summary: Cuba's national dog, a cheerful little companion with a silky coat, descended from the Bichon family.
funFacts: It's the national dog of Cuba.
Most modern Havanese descend from about 11 dogs brought out of Cuba after the revolution.

Ibizan Hound.summary: A lean, deer-like hound from the Spanish island of Ibiza, bred to hunt rabbits using sight, scent and hearing.
funFacts: Ibizan Hounds can leap remarkably high from a standstill.
Their large, upright ears help them pinpoint prey hiding in brush.

Icelandic Sheepdog.summary: Iceland's only native dog, a cheerful spitz brought over by the Vikings more than 1,000 years ago.
funFacts: It arrived in Iceland with Viking settlers between 874 and 930 AD.
Many have double dewclaws on their hind legs.

Irish Red and White Setter.summary: The older of Ireland's two setters, a red-and-white bird dog that was nearly lost as the solid-red Irish Setter grew popular.
funFacts: It predates the all-red Irish Setter.
The breed was close to extinction by the early 1900s and was revived in the 1920s.

Irish Setter.summary: A glamorous mahogany-red bird dog from Ireland, known for its boundless energy and friendly nature.
funFacts: Disney's Big Red (1962) starred an Irish Setter.
Richard Nixon's Irish Setter, King Timahoe, lived in the White House.

Irish Terrier.summary: A fiery, red-coated Irish terrier nicknamed the "Daredevil," used as a farm dog, guard and ratter.
funFacts: Irish Terriers carried messages for soldiers in World War I.
It's one of the oldest terrier breeds.

Irish Water Spaniel.summary: The tallest spaniel, a curly, liver-coated Irish water retriever with a distinctive smooth tail.
funFacts: Its thin, smooth tail earned it the nickname "rat tail."
It's often called the clown of the spaniel family.

Irish Wolfhound.summary: The tallest of all dog breeds, an ancient Irish sighthound once used to hunt wolves and in war, now a gentle giant.
funFacts: It's the tallest AKC breed; males stand at least 32 inches at the shoulder.
Despite their history as war dogs, Wolfhounds are famously gentle and easygoing.

Italian Greyhound.summary: A miniature sighthound beloved by Renaissance nobility, with all of a Greyhound's grace in a much smaller package.
funFacts: Frederick the Great of Prussia loved his Italian Greyhounds and was buried near them.
Small greyhounds like these appear in art from ancient Rome and Pompeii.

Jack Russell Terrier.summary: A small, tireless fox-hunting terrier developed by the Reverend John "Jack" Russell in 19th-century England.
funFacts: Eddie on the TV show Frasier was played by a Jack Russell named Moose.
The AKC recognizes two related breeds: the Parson Russell Terrier and the Russell Terrier.

Japanese Chin.summary: An aristocratic toy breed long cherished by Japanese nobility, known for its cat-like grace and charm.
funFacts: Many Chins do the "Chin spin," twirling in circles when excited.
Commodore Perry is said to have brought Chins back from Japan in the 1850s, some as gifts for Queen Victoria.

Japanese Spitz.summary: A small, fluffy white spitz developed in Japan in the 1920s and 1930s from German Spitz ancestors.
funFacts: It looks like a miniature Samoyed but is a separate breed.
Its stand-off white coat is surprisingly good at shedding dirt.

Keeshond.summary: A fluffy Dutch spitz with distinctive "spectacles" around its eyes, once the watchdog of barges on Dutch canals.
funFacts: It was the symbol of the Dutch Patriot party in the 1780s, named after its leader Kees de Gyselaer.
The dark lines from its eyes to its ears look like spectacles.

Kerry Blue Terrier.summary: An Irish all-purpose farm terrier whose soft, wavy coat turns blue-gray as it matures.
funFacts: Puppies are born black; the coat clears to blue between about 6 and 24 months.
It's often called the national terrier of Ireland.

Komondor.summary: A large Hungarian livestock guardian covered in white, corded "dreadlocks" that let it blend in with the flock.
funFacts: A mature Komondor's cords can reach the ground and weigh around 15 pounds.
The coat camouflages it among sheep and protects it from wolf bites.

Kuvasz.summary: A large, white Hungarian guardian dog once kept by royalty to protect estates and livestock.
funFacts: King Matthias I of Hungary reportedly trusted his Kuvaszok more than his human bodyguards.
Its white coat helped shepherds tell it apart from wolves at night.

Labradoodle.summary: A cross between a Labrador Retriever and a Poodle, first bred in Australia in 1989 as a low-shedding guide dog.
funFacts: Wally Conron bred the first Labradoodle at Royal Guide Dogs Victoria for a blind woman whose husband was allergic to dogs.
Conron later said he regretted starting the "designer dog" craze.

Labrador Retriever.summary: A friendly, outgoing retriever from Newfoundland, refined in Britain, and for decades America's most popular dog breed.
funFacts: Labs were America's most popular breed for 31 years in a row (1991–2021).
Webbed toes and a thick "otter tail" that works like a rudder make them great swimmers.

Lakeland Terrier.summary: A compact, wire-coated terrier from England's Lake District, bred to protect sheep from foxes.
funFacts: A Lakeland named Stingray won Best in Show at both Crufts (1967) and Westminster (1968).
It was bred to work in the rocky fells where foxes raided sheep.

Leonberger.summary: A giant, gentle German companion bred in the town of Leonberg, with a lion-like mane and a love of water.
funFacts: Breeder Heinrich Essig is said to have created it to resemble the lion on Leonberg's coat of arms.
Leonbergers have webbed feet and are used in water rescue.

Lhasa Apso.summary: An ancient Tibetan breed that guarded Buddhist monasteries from the inside, alerting monks to intruders.
funFacts: Tibetans called it "Abso Seng Kye" — the bark lion sentinel dog.
The Dalai Lama traditionally gave Lhasa Apsos as gifts to visiting dignitaries.

Lowchen.summary: A small, lively companion whose traditional "lion trim" earned it the nickname "little lion dog."
funFacts: "Löwchen" is German for "little lion."
In 1973 it was listed as one of the rarest dog breeds in the world.

Maltese.summary: An ancient toy breed with a floor-length white coat, pampered as a lapdog since the days of ancient Greece and Rome.
funFacts: The Maltese has been a pampered pet for more than 2,000 years.
It has no undercoat, so it sheds very little.

Maltipoo.summary: A cross between a Maltese and a toy or miniature Poodle, bred as a small, lower-shedding companion.
funFacts: Many Maltipoos keep a puppy-like look their whole lives.
Their small size makes them a popular choice for apartment living.

Manchester Terrier.summary: A sleek black-and-tan terrier developed in Manchester, England, to kill rats and chase rabbits.
funFacts: It comes in two varieties: Standard and Toy.
The tan markings on its front legs include black "thumbprints."

Mastiff.summary: A massive, ancient English guardian, one of the heaviest dog breeds in the world, with a calm, dignified nature.
funFacts: An English Mastiff named Zorba weighed 343 pounds in 1989, a record for the heaviest dog.
Mastiffs are said to have come to America on the Mayflower.

Miniature Pinscher.summary: A small, sleek German toy dog nicknamed the "King of Toys" for its confident, high-stepping strut.
funFacts: It isn't a mini Doberman: the Min Pin is the older breed.
Its high-stepping walk is called a "hackney gait," like a carriage horse's.

Miniature Schnauzer.summary: The smallest schnauzer, a bearded German farm dog bred to catch rats, now a popular family companion.
funFacts: It was developed by crossing Standard Schnauzers with smaller breeds like the Affenpinscher.
Its bushy beard and eyebrows give it a wise old-man look.

Neapolitan Mastiff.summary: A massive Italian guardian with heavy wrinkles and loose skin, descended from the war dogs of ancient Rome.
funFacts: Fang, Hagrid's dog in the Harry Potter films, was played by Neapolitan Mastiffs.
Its loose skin and folds were thought to protect it from bites.

Newfoundland.summary: A giant, sweet-natured Canadian working dog bred to help fishermen haul nets and rescue people from the sea.
funFacts: A Newfoundland named Seaman traveled with the Lewis and Clark expedition.
Nana, the nursemaid dog in Peter Pan, is a Newfoundland.
Webbed feet and a water-resistant coat make them powerful swimmers.

Norfolk Terrier.summary: One of the smallest working terriers, a sturdy little ratter from East Anglia with folded ears.
funFacts: It's nearly identical to the Norwich Terrier, except its ears fold down.
Norfolks and Norwiches were shown as one breed until 1964 in the UK.

Norwegian Buhund.summary: A Nordic spitz-type farm dog used for centuries to herd sheep and guard homesteads.
funFacts: Remains of Buhund-type dogs have been found in Viking graves.
"Bu" refers to the farm or homestead in Norwegian.

Norwegian Elkhound.summary: An ancient Norwegian hunting spitz bred to track moose and hold them at bay with loud barking.
funFacts: "Elkhound" comes from the Norwegian "elghund" — moose dog.
It's often called Norway's national dog.

Norwegian Lundehund.summary: A rare, flexible Norwegian spitz bred to climb sea cliffs and pull puffins from their nests.
funFacts: It has six toes on each foot.
It can tip its head backward to touch its spine and spread its front legs straight out to the sides.

Norwich Terrier.summary: A tiny, prick-eared English terrier bred to hunt rats and foxes, known for its fearless, cheerful attitude.
funFacts: It's the prick-eared twin of the Norfolk Terrier.
A Norwich won Best in Show at Westminster in 1998.
